# Reading practice

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/setup.R")
```

Can you say what a plot will look like from its sentence alone? The last
chapter gave you the vocabulary, and this one practices reading with it. Ten
plots follow, ending in a cube. For each one, read the sentence aloud before
looking at the picture, then check the picture against what you said. The
sentence read aloud is given under each plot. Try to say it yourself first.

## Gold medals by country {#gold-medals-by-country}

Which country won the most gold, and by how much? `medals` holds one row per
country, with its counts of gold, silver and bronze:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(medals)
```

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold)
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold."* A bar measures an
amount from zero, so the amount needs a continuous axis and the category takes
the other one. The bindings put countries on `x` and gold on `y`. There is
no transform here. `bar` draws the numbers exactly as the table gives them.

## The same bars, horizontal {#the-same-bars-horizontal}

A medal table is usually printed as a list, with the leader at the top. The
same five counts can be read that way. `medals` already lists the countries by
gold, and the first row is drawn at the top, so the leader comes first.

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(gold) + y(country)
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is gold, y is country."* Put the category on the
vertical axis and the amount on the horizontal one, and the bars become
horizontal. There is no "horizontal bar" atom,
and no argument that turns the bars. The sentence already says which axis holds
the category, so the orientation follows from the bindings.

## One measurement's shape {#one-measurements-shape}

The first two plots drew five counts that were already in the table. Often a
table holds only measurements, and no counts.

Do petal lengths gather around one typical value, or do they separate into
groups? One column, petal length, answers that, and it comes from a new table.
`iris_flowers` holds one row per flower: three measurements (sepal length,
sepal width and petal length), and the species the flower belongs to.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_flowers)
```

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length."* The `*`
attaches the transform `bin` to `bar`. `bin` divides the axis into bins and
counts the rows in each, and `bar` draws one bar per bin. A plot like this is a
**histogram**. You did not bind `y`. `bin` writes the counts itself, so the `y`
axis is labeled `Count`. Note the two peaks. Plot eight explains them.

## The same question, smoothly {#the-same-question-smoothly}

A histogram draws the distribution as flat-topped bars, one per bin, and
sometimes you want one smooth curve instead. The measurement this time is life
expectancy, across the 142 countries in `gapminder_2007`.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is life."* The question is
the same as the histogram's: how is this measurement distributed? The answer is
drawn differently. `density` replaces `bin`, and `line` replaces `bar`, because
a smooth estimate is one curve, not many bars.

## One strip of dots per continent {#one-strip-of-dots-per-continent}

The density curve in plot four reduced 142 countries to one shape. Do the
continents differ in life expectancy, and how widely do the countries
inside each one vary? Both answers are visible when every country is shown.

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is continent, y is life."* A categorical `x`
gives each category a slot on the axis, and that category's points are drawn in a
vertical strip at that slot. The same rule placed bars on country slots in plot one.
Here it applies to a different mark. A plot shaped like this one has a name: the
**strip plot**.

## The typical value per continent {#the-typical-value-per-continent}

You often want one number per continent, its average, instead of 142 separate
values.

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life."*
Each bar is one continent's average. Unlike `bin`, which writes `y` itself,
`mean` needs a column to average, and `y(life)` names it.

## Five countries across the decades {#five-countries-across-the-decades}

Plots four to six show only 2007. A question about change needs many years,
so the next plot uses another table.

How has life expectancy changed since 1952, and did five Asian countries
change at the same rate? `gapminder_asia` holds one row per country *and
year*, so each country appears twelve times, once every five years.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_asia)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + color(country)
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, color by country."*
A categorical `color` first *splits* the rows into one group per category
(here, one line per country), then colors them. One channel does two things, and you write it
once.

## Three species on one axis {#three-species-on-one-axis}

Plot three showed two peaks in petal length, and the table has three species.
How do three species make two peaks?

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, color by
species."* The left peak is setosa alone. The right peak is versicolor and
virginica together, because their petal lengths overlap. All three histograms
use the same bin edges, and each species has bars only in the bins its own
values fall into. Each fill is translucent inside an opaque outline, so every histogram stays
visible. `color` splits the rows here into one histogram per species,
by the same rule as in plot seven.

## One panel per continent {#one-panel-per-continent}

Richer countries live longer across the world as a whole, as the first chapter
showed. Is that also true inside each continent?

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) | facet(continent)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, split into
panel columns by continent."* Inside every continent except Oceania, which has
only two countries here, life expectancy also rises with income. The rise is clearest in Europe and Asia and least clear in Africa,
where the points are most scattered. The `|` operator splits the plot into panels
side by side, one panel per category. All the panels share one pair of scales, so
they can be compared; `free = TRUE` on a position fits that axis to each panel
instead ([Faceting](faceting.qmd)). As in the first chapter, `scale = "log"`
spreads out the poorer countries, which would otherwise be pressed together at
the left edge.

## Three measurements on three axes {#three-measurements-on-three-axes}

Petal length alone left two species overlapping in plot eight. Two more
measurements, sepal length and sepal width, might separate them, if all three measurements can be seen at once.

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(sepal_length) + y(sepal_width) + z(petal_length) +
  color(species)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is sepal width, z is petal
length, color by species."* Drawing in three dimensions needs no other package
and no other mark. `z` is one more position channel, and the same sentence
without `z(petal_length)` would draw a flat scatter. In the web edition the cube
turns with a drag: drag right and the side facing you moves right, drag down and
it tips down to show you the top. Every angle hides some points and shows others, so turn the cube more
than once.

## What you just did {#what-you-just-did}

Those ten plots used thirteen words: `data`, `bar`, `point`, `line`, `bin`,
`density`, `mean`, `x`, `y`, `z`, `color`, `facet`, and the scale `log`. Every plot reads in the
same order: *data, mark, positions*, then any refinements. A transform joined
the mark and a facet came last, exactly where the first chapter put them. The
same `color` split the bars and lines, and colored the points. The same `*`
attached `bin`, `mean` and `density`, which derived counts, means and
densities. Each word meant the same thing in every plot that used it.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

Every sentence here was already written, so nothing asked you to choose a mark.
[Writing practice](writing.qmd) reverses that: it starts from a question and asks
you to write the sentence.
